searchText: That's very cool! My audit stuff above was somewhat agents free-styling the mapping. How do you keep that up to date? Hey, it uses specrefs e.g. https://github.com/Consensys/teku/tree/master/specrefs which are based on ethspecify schemas https://github.com/ethereum/ethspecify they are static and maintained by clients so not up to date always, basically grab latest commit from each client for these files Agents could be more accurate I presume for filling the gaps Oh this is really neat! And yeah, not all clients have specrefs yet. I have been chatting with <@602753420033785856> from Lighthouse about it, but they're skeptical of their value. And [we made a branch](https://github.com/0xTylerHolmes/nimbus-eth2/tree/add-specrefs) with some specrefs for Nimbus (cc <@654267572107083777>) but never completed it & therefore never made the PR 😢 I don't understand this, the .yml file just seems to be a copy of the various Python spec functions? It's auto-generated. You bump the version, re-run, and it updates everything. It will also add new spec items to the files. It's just a convinient way of keeping track of spec changes. https://github.com/ethereum/ethspecify interesting You could also have these as inline comments in your codebase. But most clients seem to prefer centralized files. like, have the Python code as an inline comment? Yup. I can find an example. https://github.com/OffchainLabs/prysm/blob/9ec345e0fda9439740ac564eefb3a9173ead3cf5/beacon-chain/core/gloas/builder_exit.go#L10-L33 that's not easily enough parseable/distinguishable enough really what is this `hash` from/of? Nimbus already links systematically to the spec reference URL available checked for any given function, in a more human-readable way when feasible, i.e. 1.7.0-alpha.7 (sometimes it's not yet in a spec release and we have to use a commithash). I'm not sure this system would 100% replace this, because while some spec functions translate 1:1, some cannot, and the more important information is when we've checked the equivalence, not what the upstream function looks like (which is already accessible) I used to use a script to automate updating to these: https://github.com/status-im/nimbus-eth2/blob/stable/scripts/find_unchanged_consensus_spec_files.sh That's just `sha256(python code)`. It's there to detect any changes. In your codebase, you have just this (`<spec fn="apply_deposit" fork="electra" hash="c723ce7b" />`) and if the hash changes you know something change but would need to reference the spec to see what exactly. ok, this seems like it could be a more precise version of that for some of those. But we also use those spec references for non-just-Python-code-equivalence, but as a general pointer into the specs for English prose the issue with that script is that a lot of AI-driven refactoring (+ other random cosmetic line-ending changes, etc lots of just pointless noise) ended up being used across all the files with enough regularity it got tedious need AI to ingest AI I guess No AI with ethspecify. It's deterministic. You might like some of the others styles btw. Eg: * https://github.com/ethereum/ethspecify#link * https://github.com/ethereum/ethspecify#diff If you're interested you should look into using it in your codebase. I can help if you want, but probably best to just let you guys handle it. yeah, we use something similar to the link style now it could be a good way to make that more maintainable and even if it only applied to some subset of them that would still be useful I do have some concern about the longevity of these links Yes me too. I was just thinking about that. i.e. the GitHub URLs we use are designed to go down only in case of basically catastrophe I'm wanting to transfer that website to a different domain in the future. To something more stable. Like `consensus.ethereum.foundation/specs` we specifically link certain tags/commits for example, not trunk branches So I actually wouldn't suggest using the link style right now. Unless you're okay with a big change later. and the GitHub repo could disappear but that would be unlikely, usually they're just abandoned yeah, so I like the concept but would want the metadata aspect more parseable (not inline) and set up not only for internal spec-maintenance per se, but also as a kind of documentation (as it is now) for why-do-we-even-have-this-code i.e. to show that it maps to a spec thing in a _summarized_, human-readable way, not only for people/machines checking for equivalence because we maintain/manage functions different if they're spec (we try to keep it 1:1 matching if feasible) vs non-spec (up to us) If you explore using this & notice something you'd like to change, ping me and I can probably accommodate. alright, sure actually, I guess, more parseable != not inline. they're different things

excerpts.author: stefanbratanov
excerpts.content: Hey, it uses specrefs e.g. https://github.com/Consensys/teku/tree/master/specrefs which are based on ethspecify schemas https://github.com/ethereum/ethspecify they are static and maintained by clients so not up to date always, basically grab latest commit from each client for these files
